pitch: How our mind judges and decides, why it errs in predictable ways, and how to decide better.
br: effort · control · the bat and ball
What you see is all there is
Small numbers and regression to the mean
what you own · selling price · status quo
Case study: the project going off track
quiz: It is fast, automatic and cannot be switched off
It produces most of our impressions and intuitions, but makes systematic errors.
A bat and a ball cost $1.10. The bat costs $1 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?
If the ball cost 10 cents, the bat would cost $1.10 and the total $1.20. System 2 needs to check.
What does “what you see is all there is” mean?
You must see everything to decide
We judge with the information available without considering what is missing
A coherent story built from little information seems very convincing to us.
The influence of a first number, even arbitrary, on an estimate
Even a rigged wheel of fortune or dice influenced estimates, including those of experienced judges.
What does Kahneman recommend against the planning fallacy?
Start from the outside view: the actual results of comparable projects
The inside view ignores the unexpected; the reference class gives a realistic baseline.
The fact that a loss weighs about twice as much as an equivalent gain
It explains in particular resistance to change: what you lose is more visible than what you gain.
You imagine the project has failed a year from now and everyone writes down why
It legitimizes expressing doubts and surfaces risks no one had considered.
When is an expert's intuition reliable?
In a regular environment, after long practice with fast feedback
Only if they have a degree
An expert's confidence tells you nothing: look at the environment and the experience.
